strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-documented gap: large-scale, instance-annotated, materials-oriented electron micrograph data with paired text. UniEM-3M (5,091 raw EMs, ~3M instance masks, structured attribute descriptions) is substantially larger and denser than prior EM segmentation datasets (EMPS, Okunev, Bals et al.), and Table 1 clearly positions it against existing resources.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully engineered for the extreme instance density of EMs: a bespoke web-based annotation platform, iterative human-in-the-loop pseudo-labeling, and a multi-stage quality-control process (peer review plus expert audit). Supplementary details on the platform and prompt design for LLM-assisted structured descriptions support reproducibility of the data-construction methodology.

The benchmark is comprehensive and well-organized: representative anchor-based, anchor-free, center-based, and flow-based methods are retrained and compared on sensible sparse/dense splits, with results supporting a clear, evidence-backed conclusion that flow-based approaches are better suited to high-density micrographs.

The release package is multifaceted for a dataset paper: a public data subset, a full benchmark, a strong baseline (UniEM-Net), and a fine-tuned text-to-image diffusion model that serves both as an augmentation engine and a privacy-preserving proxy for the unreleased data. The generative model's utility is validated quantitatively (FID, style similarity) and by downstream pretraining/finetuning experiments (Table 3, Fig. 6).

Appropriate contribution type: this is a Datasets/Benchmarks paper with an applied baseline; the value is judged primarily on dataset quality, benchmark rigor, and community utility, all of which are solid. The dataset and benchmark likely to have meaningful impact on automated materials analysis and future materials-oriented vision-language research.
weaknesses: Only a subset of the dataset is publicly released; the full UniEM-3M is not, and the diffusion model is offered as a 'proxy' for the withheld distribution. This limits external verification of headline claims (e.g., the 3M-instance count, annotation quality, and the full benchmark results), which is a meaningful issue for a dataset paper whose primary artifact is the data itself.

Data provenance and licensing are insufficiently addressed. The dataset aggregates web-crawled images and images from prior public datasets, yet there is no discussion of copyright/licensing status, terms of redistribution, or an ethics/consent statement—particularly important given the paper's own emphasis on privacy as a motivation for the diffusion-based surrogate.

Annotation quality is asserted rather than quantified. There are no reported inter-annotator agreement statistics, expert-vs-pseudo-label IoU estimates, or a sampled re-annotation audit to characterize label noise. Since ~3M labels were produced by model-assisted refinement, quantitative quality evidence would substantially strengthen the benchmark's credibility.

UniEM-Net's technical novelty is limited: it is an adaptation of Cellpose-style flow-field segmentation with a SAM-ViT backbone, and the methodology section is thin (the 'energy function' and 'modified Euler integration scheme' are described only qualitatively). No ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual design choices versus simply fine-tuning CellViT/Cellpose-SAM longer or on more data.

Comparison fairness concerns: UniEM-Net is trained for 180,000 iterations with a custom pipeline while baselines are fine-tuned for 72 epochs with 'default settings' plus minimal modifications; anchor-based methods are excluded from the dense split entirely (Table 2 shows '-' entries), so the claim of superiority in dense scenes rests on an incomplete set of competitors.

The 'universal' framing is somewhat overstated: over 90% of images are SEM with limited TEM/other modalities, and material categories follow a long-tailed distribution. Additionally, evaluation is restricted to a single test split of the same dataset; there is no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution generalization experiment for the segmentation baseline.

Minor presentation issues: the style-similarity metric is ad hoc and defined only in passing; some figures (e.g., t-SNE in Fig. 7) are qualitative and could support alternative interpretations; the writing contains minor grammatical irregularities that occasionally obscure meaning.

strengths: The dataset addresses a genuine gap: existing materials-EM datasets are either tiny, classification-only, or literature-derived (post-processed images), so a large raw-experimental collection with ~3M instance masks and structured attribute-level text is a meaningful resource for the materials-vision community.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully engineered: a custom high-performance web annotation platform, iterative model-in-the-loop labeling with human refinement, and multi-stage quality control (peer review plus expert audit) are appropriate for the extreme instance density of electron micrographs.

The benchmark covers a reasonable spread of instance segmentation paradigms (anchor-based, anchor-free, center/contour-based, flow-based), and the observation that natural-image models degrade under extreme instance density is a useful empirical finding.

The text-to-image diffusion model released as both an augmentation tool and a privacy-preserving proxy for the unreleased portion of the data is an interesting idea, supported by FID/style consistency analysis and downstream segmentation experiments (Tab. 3, Fig. 6).
weaknesses: Partial data release undermines the central claim. The full 5,091 images and 3M instance labels are not released; only 'a subset' will be public, with the diffusion model offered as a 'proxy for the complete data distribution.' A generated proxy is not a substitute for real labeled data: the benchmark cannot be independently verified, the train/test split cannot be checked for contamination (especially since web-crawled and diffusion-augmented data may overlap), and results on the full UniEM-3M are not reproducible by the community. This is a consequential shortcoming for a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution.

The comparison validating UniEM-Net is not clearly fair. UniEM-Net's data engine itself used diffusion augmentation during annotation, and the paper states the SOTA baseline 'combines generated and real micrographs,' whereas the baselines in Tab. 2 are trained only on real data. Additionally, UniEM-Net is trained for 180,000 iterations on 4 GPUs while baselines are fine-tuned for 72 epochs; the training budgets and data conditions are not aligned, so the large gap in Tab. 2 (e.g., 0.824 vs. 0.605 mAP for Cellpose-SAM) may partly reflect training regime and data rather than architectural advantage.

UniEM-Net offers limited technical novelty. It is essentially a Cellpose-style flow-based segmentation approach on a SAM-ViT-base backbone. The methodology section is vague: the 'energy function,' 'modified Euler integration scheme,' and refinement step are described only at a high level, with no ablations isolating which components produce the gains over CellViT/Cellpose-SAM.

Annotation quality is asserted but not quantified. Most of the 3M masks originate as model pseudo-labels refined by volunteers; no inter-annotator agreement, estimated mask error rate, or accuracy of pseudo-label refinement is reported. Similarly, the structured text attributes are produced by GPT/Gemini with expert review only for flagged discrepancies; the fraction of attributes requiring correction and residual label noise is unknown. For a benchmark paper, this is a significant evidential gap.

The 'universal' framing is overstated. The supplementary material reveals the dataset is >90% SEM with limited TEM coverage, and the material/density distributions are heavily long-tailed. Generality across the EM spectrum is claimed but not demonstrated (e.g., no cross-modality or cross-source generalization experiments).

Several baselines are omitted from the dense subset (all '-' entries for anchor-based and YOLACT/Mask2Former in Tab. 2) due to claimed computational issues. This weakens the benchmark's completeness precisely where the paper's main argument (flow methods excel in dense scenes) is made; approximate or chunked NMS variants could have been attempted.

Evaluation of the generative model is methodologically weak. FID is computed with Inception features, which are poorly suited to grayscale microscopy texture; the 'Style' metric (cosine similarity of DINO CLS tokens) is ad hoc and unvalidated; and the reported comparison in Tab. 4 (Real Data FID 28.06 vs. training set) is confusing and lacks statistical grounding. No human or expert evaluation of generated-image realism is provided.

Provenance, licensing, and ethical issues around the data (academic collaborations, web crawling, reuse of the Aversa et al. 2018 subset) are not discussed. There is no limitations section and no meaningful societal-impact discussion, which matters given the stated privacy-motivation for the generative surrogate.

Presentation and rigor issues: mixed training metrics (mAP@0.5 and PQ@0.5 only, no standard AP@[.5:.95]); Fig. 4/5 visual comparisons are hard to parse at scale; the paper is not formatted per the venue template; and portions of the writing are imprecise (e.g., contradictory statements about which training set yields the reported results).

strengths: As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the paper addresses a genuine gap: existing materials-EM resources either lack instance-level masks (Aversa, Stuckner, MMSci) or cover too few images/scenes (EMPS, Okunev, Bals). UniEM-3M's ~3 million instance labels across 5,091 raw experimental micrographs, with per-image structured attribute descriptions, is a substantially scaled and differentiated resource relative to Tab. 1, and the claim of extreme instance density (images exceeding 2,000 instances) is convincingly evidenced by the statistics in Fig. 3 and supplementary Fig. 12.

The data engine is well documented: multi-source collection with deduplication and GPT-based quality filtering, YOLO-based removal of embedded metadata text, a dual-LLM (Gemini + GPT) cross-validation pipeline for structured attribute extraction with expert arbitration, and a bespoke high-density annotation platform with a clear iterative human-in-the-loop workflow and multi-stage QC (supplementary Sec. 7–8). This level of procedural detail supports reproducibility and trust in the labels.

The benchmark is reasonably broad, covering anchor-based, anchor-free, center/flow-based, and interactive paradigms, and the sparse/dense split analysis yields a substantive scientific finding: detection-based pipelines fail on extreme density while 2D-flow methods remain robust — a useful takeaway beyond the specific baseline.

The generative component is validated with both quantitative (FID, DINO-based style similarity, t-SNE overlap) and downstream evidence (Tab. 3 showing generated data alone approximates 1–2K real images; Fig. 6 showing Gen30K pretraining beats SA1B pretraining across finetune sizes), supporting the claimed dual role as augmentation tool and privacy-preserving data proxy.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, and the supplementary material (prompts, implementation details, extended visualizations, qualitative per-method analysis) is thorough.
weaknesses: Partial public release weakens the central contribution: only a subset of images, labels, and text will be open, with the full distribution represented only by a generative proxy. For a dataset paper whose headline value is the data itself, this materially limits reproducibility, external benchmarking on the full set, and verification of the reported results by the community. The rationale (privacy) is stated but the fraction released and any licensing/redistribution analysis of the web-crawled portion are not specified.

UniEM-Net is under-specified and its novelty is hard to assess: Sec. 3.1 describes a Cellpose-inspired flow formulation with a modified Euler integration scheme and SAM-ViT-base backbone, but gives no equations, architectural details, or ablations isolating the claimed contributions (energy function, skeleton/boundary integration, semantic-probability fusion). The margin over Cellpose-SAM on dense PQ@0.5 is small (0.703 vs 0.700), and the much larger sparse gap (0.824 vs 0.605) is not explained mechanistically; without ablations, it is unclear whether gains stem from the design or simply from training on the full dataset.

Benchmark fairness is uneven: anchor-based methods are trained and evaluated only on the sparse subset while field-based methods run on both, and backbones/parameter budgets differ (Cellpose-SAM uses ViT-large at 304M vs UniEM-Net at 93M). Table 2 also contains many unexplained dashes, and the metrics section defines PQ at 0.5 in a non-standard way that deserves clarification.

Label quality is asserted rather than measured. Since the majority of masks originate as pseudo-labels refined by annotators (some of whom are 'trained volunteers' rather than domain experts), the paper would be strengthened by quantitative inter-annotator agreement, mask-accuracy audits on a held-out expert subset, or estimated label noise — particularly given that pseudo-label errors could be systematically inherited by the diffusion model and by UniEM-Net evaluations.

Universality claims are somewhat overstated: supplementary Fig. 11 shows >90% SEM and only ~3.7% TEM, so 'universal' coverage across EM modalities is limited; the coarse categorical scheme for attributes also reduces the precision of the claimed attribute disentanglement.

Circularity concerns: the diffusion model used to augment annotation training data, and the generative model evaluated in Sec. 5.2, are entangled with the dataset construction pipeline; FID is computed against the generative training set itself, which favors the fine-tuned model and limits the strength of the distribution-consistency claim.

Minor but noticeable polish issues (e.g., 'GPT-o4-mini', 'SDXL finetune' heading, inconsistent metric formatting in Tab. 2, some ungrammatical sentences) and missing discussion of societal/ethical considerations for web-crawled scientific imagery beyond a brief privacy motivation.

strengths: Substantial and clearly valuable dataset contribution (Datasets/Benchmarks type): 5,091 raw experimental EMs with ~3M instance masks is an order-of-magnitude increase in annotated instance density over prior materials-EM datasets (Tab. 1), and the combination of pixel-level masks with structured, attribute-disentangled textual descriptions fills a genuine gap relative to MMSci-style literature-sourced resources.

The annotation pipeline is carefully engineered and unusually well documented for a dataset paper: a bespoke high-density annotation platform, multi-stage QC with peer review and expert audit, and a quantitative reliability study (Tab. 2) reporting Krippendorff's Alpha and PQ for inter-annotator agreement and across pipeline stages, which allows readers to judge annotation quality rather than take it on faith.

The benchmark is broad and informative: twelve representative methods spanning two-stage, one-stage, query-based, and bottom-up paradigms are evaluated with domain-standard metrics (mAP, PQ), and the supplementary analysis (Fig. 12 memory study; Sec. 14.2) empirically justifies why detection/query-based methods are benchmarked on a sparse subset.

The generative component is evaluated with more rigor than typical augmentation papers: a domain-specific FID reference baseline (28.06), a DINO-based style score, t-SNE comparison, and—most importantly—downstream evidence showing 30K synthetic images approach 3K real images and that Gen+Real training improves results (Tab. 4, Fig. 6a, Tab. 5).

Cross-dataset zero-shot and finetuned evaluation on EMPS and Okunev et al. supports the claim that EM3M is harder and more representative than prior benchmarks, and the honest 'Open Problems' section (e.g., PQ@90 dropping to 0.340, human-vs-model gap 0.786 vs 0.704) strengthens scientific credibility.

Public release of the dataset, generative engine, and demo supports reproducibility and community reuse; supplementary material covers prompts, implementation details, and per-attribute statistics needed for reproduction.
weaknesses: Benchmark comparability is asymmetric: detection- and query-based methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset with default settings (100-instance cap, 'out-of-the-box' configs), while bottom-up methods including UniAIMS use the full dataset and tailored engineering. Numbers in Tab. 3 are therefore not directly comparable across classes, and the claimed superiority of the bottom-up family conflates architectural suitability with evaluation-protocol differences. The justification is reasonable but the headline comparison should be interpreted with caution.

UniAIMS's advantage over Cellpose is partly a training-budget effect: Cellpose is trained on a single GPU at 256x256 with its size model, while UniAIMS uses multi-GPU training, larger inputs, LSJ augmentation, and a ViT-Base backbone. A budget- or resolution-matched Cellpose ablation is not reported, so the architectural vs. resource attribution of the gains remains unclear.

Potential circularity in the annotation loop: the diffusion model was trained on EM3M-style data and used to augment training of the segmentation model that produced pseudo-labels for the dataset itself. This could inject correlated model bias into labels; the pseudo-label PQ of 0.553 (Tab. 2) indicates substantial initial error, and while human refinement helps, the paper does not quantify residual systematic bias on non-subset images.

Textual annotations are not quantitatively validated: the nine-attribute descriptions come from Gemini/GPT with human review, but no error rate, agreement statistic, or per-attribute accuracy for the final released captions is reported, unlike the segmentation masks. Since the text modality is a headline contribution ('multimodal dataset'), this is a notable evidence gap.

Data provenance and licensing for the ~10% web-crawled images are addressed only briefly; redistribution rights for crawled micrographs are a practical reproducibility/legal concern that deserves more explicit treatment.

The dataset is still modest in image count (5,091) and heavily skewed toward SEM (~85-90%) with a long-tail material distribution; claims of 'universality' should be tempered, though the released statistics make the skew transparent.

Minor presentation issues: Tab. 3 mixes sparse-subset and full-dataset results in one table without visual separation; some references appear questionable (future-dated arXiv entries, e.g., refs 27 and 60 dated 2026 with implausible IDs), which slightly undermines citation hygiene.

strengths: Substantial curation effort: EM3M provides 5,091 raw experimental electron micrographs with ~3M instance masks and structured, disentangled textual descriptions, which the comparison table (Tab. 1) plausibly shows fills a real gap relative to existing small or literature-derived EM datasets.

The multi-stage quality-control narrative is unusually thorough for this area: inter-annotator agreement (KA ~0.81-0.82, PQ ~0.78) on a re-annotated stratified subset, staged evaluation of pseudo-label → peer review → final validation, and an Open Problems section that candidly reports weak boundary quality (PQ@90 = 0.340 vs. 0.704 at @50) and the gap to human agreement (0.786).

The benchmark covers four segmentation paradigms with reasonable implementation reporting (codebases, optimizers, schedules in Supp. Sec. 14), and the memory analysis (Fig. 12) gives a concrete, empirical justification for why dense-instance training is intractable for top-down methods.

The synthetic-data evaluation is more careful than typical: 30K generated images reach performance comparable to ~3K real images, FID is contextualized against a domain-specific augmentation reference rather than reported raw, and pretraining on generated data is compared against an SA1B-pretrained control.
Release of the dataset, generative engine, and baseline, plus supplementary prompts and annotation-platform details, supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark fairness is questionable. Detection/query-based methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset, while bottom-up methods (including the authors' UniAIMS) run on the full dataset; moreover Cellpose is trained at 256×256 on a single GPU with default settings, whereas UniAIMS uses multi-GPU distributed training, a ViT-B backbone, and LSJ augmentation. The headline claim that UniAIMS is SOTA (0.818 vs. Cellpose 0.711 mAP) therefore conflates architectural advantage with substantially better training configuration and data; an upgraded Cellpose or adapted query-based baseline is not provided.

Circularity in the data engine is not adequately resolved. The diffusion model is trained on EM3M images, its outputs augment the segmentation model that generates pseudo-labels for EM3M, and those pseudo-labels (PQ only 0.553 at the pseudo-label stage) become the ~3M 'ground truth' masks. The N=300 re-annotation subset is small, and model-induced bias in the bulk of the 2.7M+ masks outside this subset remains a plausible concern.

The UniAIMS contribution is explicitly 'implementation-level refinement' (multi-GPU support, removing the size model, LSJ, backbone swap). For a paper whose primary contribution type is Datasets/Benchmarks this is acceptable, but the abstract and conclusion frame UniAIMS as a strong methodological contribution, which oversells engineering adaptations of Cellpose.

Split design undermines the generalization claims. The 4,128/963 train/test split is random, so images from the same institution, instrument, or material family can appear in both; the reported cross-dataset and zero-shot results would be more convincing with a material- or source-disjoint split.

Provenance and licensing of the data are unaddressed. The paper itself cites IP/privacy restrictions as a barrier for the field, yet ~10% of images are web-crawled with no discussion of licensing, consent, or redistribution rights; the public dataset footnotes on page 1 are also empty, which is problematic for a release-focused paper.

Several references appear unreliable or irrelevant (e.g., citations [27], [60], [61] dated 2026 with topics—flow-matching rectification, diffusion acceleration, fMRI-to-gesture reconstruction—unrelated to the cited claims), raising questions about citation accuracy that should be corrected.

The text-to-image component is a fairly standard SDXL + LoRA + learnable-token recipe; its novelty is limited, and the structured-prompt design is only briefly validated (t-SNE overlap and style similarity are weak evidence of attribute controllability; no attribute-classification accuracy on generated samples is reported).

Textual descriptions are largely produced by Gemini/GPT with cross-checking and human review, but the fraction of descriptions requiring expert correction and the residual error rate after review are not reported, making the reliability of the multimodal annotation difficult to assess relative to the segmentation labels.

strengths: Significant and clearly valuable dataset contribution (Datasets/Benchmarks type): 5,091 raw experimental EMs with ~3M instance masks and structured, attribute-disentangled text descriptions fills a genuine gap in materials-science computer vision; Table 1 convincingly positions EM3M against prior resources.

Annotation quality is taken seriously: a multi-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline, three-annotator re-annotation study (KA/PQ agreement in Tab. 2), and expert validation give unusually rigorous quality evidence for this domain.

The benchmark covers four segmentation paradigms (two-stage, one-stage, query-based, bottom-up) with matched backbones where possible, and the supplementary material (RAM analysis in Sec. 14.2) empirically justifies why top-down methods fail at extreme instance densities.

The synthetic-data study is more convincing than typical augmentation claims: quantitative FID with a domain-specific reference baseline, downstream ablations (Tab. 4), pretraining comparisons against SA1B (Fig. 6a), and cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation (Tab. 5).

Honest and substantive Open Problems section (e.g., PQ@90 drop to 0.340, human-model gap of 0.08 PQ) that correctly frames the dataset as an open, unsaturated challenge rather than declaring the problem solved.
Dataset, generative engine, and demo are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility and community impact.
weaknesses: The headline benchmark comparison is not apples-to-apples: detection/query-based methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset (<100 instances) while bottom-up methods and UniAIMS are evaluated on the full set (Tab. 3). The sparse-subset columns partially mitigate this, but the 'state-of-the-art' framing rests on UniAIMS outperforming methods that never faced the dense data, and Cellpose was trained at 256×256 on a single GPU while UniAIMS uses multi-GPU distributed training at higher resolutions — a computational asymmetry that weakens fairness claims.

A large share of the ~3M masks originate as model pseudo-labels refined by annotators. Despite the quality-control pipeline, model-bias propagation into the ground truth is only indirectly assessed (validation subset N=300, 6% of test set size); the human-vs-model PQ gap (0.786 vs 0.704) suggests labels themselves may cap achievable performance, and pseudo-label statistics per density level are not reported.

Provenance and licensing of web-crawled images (~10%) are not discussed: redistribution rights, per-image licensing, and consent for the 60+ contributing institutions are unaddressed, which matters for a publicly released resource.

The AP metric definition differs from COCO-style AP; absolute numbers are therefore not comparable to the broader literature, yet phrases like 'state-of-the-art mAP of 0.818' invite such comparison without the qualifier.

Generative evaluation relies partly on weak proxies (t-SNE overlap, CLS-token style similarity); no FID/precision-recall against an established microscopy feature extractor, and no assessment of whether generated masks/images preserve physically meaningful measurement statistics (particle-size distributions), which is the actual downstream use case.

Several references appear unreliable or inconsistent with the claims they support (e.g., citations dated 2026 including an apparently unrelated fMRI and phase-mapping work listed as diffusion-model references [27, 60, 61]), raising citation-hygiene concerns.

UniAIMS itself is a modest engineering refinement of Cellpose (size-model removal, LSJ, distributed training, ViT-B backbone) — appropriate as a baseline but the ablation isolating each modification's contribution (especially backbone change vs. LSJ) is not provided in the main paper.
